finding.claim: reset_password_loose() compares the stored reset token with loose '==' against an untyped $token. If $token is a non-string value (e.g. JSON boolean true, or null) that coerces to match, the password of any account with a reset row is overwritten knowing only the email, without the token.
finding.source: $token parameter (untyped; attacker-controlled if the caller passes the JSON-decoded request body value rather than a string)
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... (reset.php:5-6)

trace.note: SELECT token FROM resets WHERE email = quote($email); fetch() returns the row or false

$row['token'] == $token: with $token === true, any non-empty stored token other than '0' compares equal; with $token === null, an empty/NULL stored token compares equal; numeric-string pairs such as '0e123' == '0e456' also compare equal (magic-hash)
password_hash($new) written to users.pw for the email, with no further check of $token

finding.guards_checked: $db->quote() on email in both SELECT and UPDATE (blocks SQLi via email under PDO); no type check on $token; no check that the token is non-empty; no expiry check; no attempt limit. Reachability of the true/null bypass depends on the caller, which is outside this directory. Severity high if the caller passes JSON values; magic-hash variant is low probability for random hex tokens.

verdict.guard_found: No guard inside reset.php. The email is quoted with $db->quote() at reset.php:3, 5-6, so SQL injection via email is blocked. $token has no type check and no non-empty check at reset.php:4. The sibling reset_password() at reset.php:12-20 uses hash_equals with a (string) cast, but reset_password_loose() does not call it. Whether the caller passes a JSON boolean or null is not visible in this directory.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: reset.php:4 uses loose == against an untyped $token and reset.php:5-6 writes the password with no further token check. But the only file in this directory is reset.php, so whether any caller passes a non-string $token (true or null) that an attacker controls is unknown, and the magic-hash variant is unlikely for random hex tokens.

finding.claim: reset_password() still accepts an empty or missing token when the stored token is NULL or '' for the account. (string)null becomes '', and hash_equals() then matches it, so a password change succeeds without knowing the token.
finding.source: $token parameter; a missing or null value is cast to '' on line 14
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... (reset.php:15-16)

trace.note: SELECT token FROM resets WHERE email = quote($email); fetch() returns the row, whose token may be NULL or ''
hash_equals($row['token'], (string)$token): (string)null === '' and hash_equals(null/'' , '') is true; the strict-looking form does not reject an empty token
password_hash($new) written to users.pw for the email

finding.guards_checked: hash_equals is constant-time and type-strict for non-empty strings, so it blocks the timing and loose-typing issues in the loose variant; $row presence is checked; $db->quote() on email. No check that $row['token'] is non-empty. Exploitability requires a resets row with a NULL or empty token, which depends on the schema and the code that creates rows (not in this directory).

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:13-14 checks only that a row was fetched ($row truthy) and then calls hash_equals($row['token'], (string)$token) with no non-empty check on the stored token or the supplied token. The only other function, reset_password_loose (reset.php:4), is a different function and is not the one the candidate describes. No other guard exists in the directory.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: reset.php:14 passes a NULL or empty stored token and an empty supplied token through to hash_equals, and reset.php:15-16 then writes the new password, so no control in this file blocks it. Whether an attacker can reach it depends on whether a resets row with a NULL or empty token exists for some email, and the schema and the code that inserts rows are not in this directory, so exploitability cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: Reset tokens are not single-use and are not invalidated. Neither function deletes or marks the resets row after a successful password change, and neither checks an expiry time, so a token that was ever valid can be replayed to change the password again.
finding.source: Any previously valid reset token that an attacker has obtained (leaked via logs, Referer, email forwarding, or a shared device)
finding.sink: Password change for the account, UPDATE users SET pw (reset.php:5-6 and 15-16)

trace.note: query selects the token for the email with no expiry column and no ORDER BY/LIMIT; fetch() returns an arbitrary row if several exist
success path updates pw but issues no DELETE FROM resets / UPDATE resets SET used
reset_password() has the same missing delete and expiry check, so the token stays valid indefinitely

finding.guards_checked: Checked for DELETE/UPDATE on resets, an expiry or created_at comparison, and single-row selection in both functions; none present in this file. Confirm whether the caller or a DB trigger removes rows. Also, with several outstanding rows per email, fetch() takes an arbitrary one, so an older token can remain valid after a newer one is issued.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:3 and :13 are bare SELECTs with no expiry or created_at check and no LIMIT/ORDER BY. reset.php:5-6 and :15-16 run only the password UPDATE, with no DELETE or UPDATE on resets. The only file in the directory is reset.php, so no caller or DB trigger is visible that would consume the row.
verdict.reason: Both reset_password_loose (reset.php:3-7) and reset_password (reset.php:13-17) update the password on a matching token and never delete or mark the resets row, so a previously valid token stays usable for another reset. Severity is limited because the attacker must already hold a token that was once valid, and a DB trigger or external cleanup job outside this directory could still remove rows.

finding.claim: Nothing in these functions limits guesses against the reset token. Each call is an unthrottled oracle that returns only true/false. If tokens have low entropy (e.g. a short numeric code), an attacker can brute-force an account's reset token and take it over.
finding.source: $token guesses supplied by an unauthenticated attacker for a known email address
finding.sink: Password change for the account (reset.php:5-6 and 15-16)

trace.note: each call performs one lookup and one comparison with no counter, lockout, or delay
the comparison result alone decides the password update, so every call is a full guess

finding.guards_checked: Both functions return false without distinguishing a missing email from a wrong token, so there is no account-enumeration oracle here. There is no rate limiting, attempt counter, or token-entropy check in this file. The real exposure depends on token generation and on any rate limiting at the HTTP layer, which are outside this directory and unverified.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only control in reset.php:14 is hash_equals(), which makes the comparison constant-time but does not limit attempts. Nothing in reset.php counts failures, locks out, or delays. The token generation code and any HTTP-layer rate limiting are not in this directory, so they could not be checked.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: reset.php:13 does one lookup, reset.php:14 alone gates the password update at reset.php:15-16, and no throttle exists in the file. Whether the attack is practical depends on the token's entropy and on any rate limiting at the HTTP layer, and neither is in this directory, so the claim can't be decided from the code available.
